headline: Stockholm is building 3,200 affordable homes — here's what you need to know
body:
Stockholm just approved 2.4 billion SEK for 3,200 new affordable homes in Järva, Skärholmen, and Farsta. 40% of units are reserved for lower-income households, and the city is shifting from a lottery to income-based allocation.

Over 42,000 households are on the waiting list. Construction starts next year, applications open January 2027. Everyone with permanent residency qualifies — no matter where they're from.

Housing policy is often framed around nuclear families, but this matters for everyone — including non-binary people navigating a housing system that rarely accounts for non-traditional household structures. Income-based allocation at least means your identity isn't the barrier — your economic situation is evaluated the same as anyone else's.

headline: Sweden's new language requirement for residency — and what it means for you
body:
From March 2027, permanent residency in Sweden requires conversational Swedish (CEFR B1). You'll be tested at SFI centres if you're a non-EU national with 3+ years on a temporary permit.

Exemptions: over 65, documented learning disabilities, refugees with subsidiary protection. About 34,000 people are in scope.

Here's what's not in the policy: any recognition that non-binary people already navigate extra bureaucratic friction — from misgendered forms to binary-only identity systems. The language test itself is gender-neutral, which is good. But the support systems around it — childcare access, workplace accommodations — are often built around assumptions that don't fit everyone. Advocating for inclusive SFI environments matters as much as the test itself.

headline: Stockholm's 2.4B SEK housing policy: structurally fair or structurally blind?
body:
Stockholm City Council allocated 2.4 billion SEK for 3,200 affordable units in Järva, Skärholmen, and Farsta, with 40% reserved for households below the median income threshold. The shift from lottery to income-linked earmarking addresses one axis of inequality — economic — while leaving others unexamined.

The 42,000-household queue underscores demand. Construction begins Q3 2026, applications January 2027. All permanent residents qualify regardless of citizenship.

The policy's household definitions rely on legal categories that often fail non-binary people: cohabitation registries, family composition assessments, and income-splitting calculations all assume binary gender pairings. While the income-linked model is identity-neutral in principle, its implementation infrastructure encodes binary assumptions. True structural fairness requires auditing these downstream mechanisms for gender-diverse exclusion patterns.

headline: CEFR B1 mandate: gender-neutral test, gender-blind infrastructure
body:
The Swedish Migration Agency's CEFR B1 proficiency requirement for permanent residency (March 2027) applies to all non-EU nationals with 3+ years on temporary permits. Testing at SFI centres, exemptions for over-65s, documented learning disabilities, and subsidiary protection refugees. ~34,000 affected.

The test itself doesn't ask your gender. But the infrastructure around it does — repeatedly. SFI registration forms, support service eligibility, and even classroom groupings often default to binary gender categories. For non-binary people, every institutional touchpoint becomes a site of potential misgendering.

The policy's silence on gender identity isn't neutrality — it's erasure by omission. Structural inclusion would mean gender-diverse intake processes, trained SFI staff, and complaint mechanisms that recognise non-binary discrimination. Until then, formal equality of the test masks substantive inequality of the system.

headline: Affordable housing at 70: where age, gender identity, and policy gaps collide
body:
Stockholm's 2.4B SEK allocation for 3,200 affordable units (Järva, Skärholmen, Farsta) reserves 40% for below-median-income households. Income-linked earmarking replaces lottery allocation. 42,000+ on the queue. Construction Q3 2026, applications January 2027.

For older non-binary people, this policy sits at a triple intersection: age-related accessibility needs, income constraints from pension systems that may not reflect a full career (especially for those who transitioned later in life), and housing systems that categorise residents by binary gender for everything from shared facilities to next-of-kin documentation.

The policy is silent on all three intersections. Age-adapted housing provisions are absent. Gender-diverse household recognition is absent. The assumption that income-linking alone creates equity ignores the compounding disadvantages that older non-binary people carry into the housing system.

headline: Language requirement at 70: the intersection of age exemptions and gender identity erasure
body:
The CEFR B1 requirement for permanent residency (March 2027) exempts applicants over 65 — which covers many older non-binary people. But the exemption's framing reveals a deeper issue: it treats age as a standalone category, ignoring how gender identity shapes the experience of ageing within immigration systems.

Non-EU nationals with 3+ years on temporary permits are in scope. SFI testing nationwide. ~34,000 affected. Additional exemptions for learning disabilities and subsidiary protection.

For non-binary seniors who do fall within scope (those under 65), the SFI system presents compounding barriers: binary registration systems, gendered classroom dynamics, and assessment environments designed without gender-diverse people in mind. The age exemption provides relief from the test but not from the system's binary architecture. True inclusion for older non-binary migrants requires both policy protection and infrastructure redesign.
